name: litellm

facts.description: The fastest, litest AI Gateway. Rust core with Python SDK. Call 100+ LLM APIs in OpenAI (or native) format with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing, and logging [Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, VertexAI, vLLM, Nvidia NIM]

title: LiteLLM: The AI Gateway for Calling 100+ LLM APIs
answer: LiteLLM is an open source AI gateway from BerriAI that lets you call over 100 LLM APIs, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Azure and VertexAI, through one OpenAI-style interface, with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing and logging. It is written in Python with a Rust core, and the one thing to know before adopting it is that the project is mid-migration to a Rust gateway, so the Python proxy you deploy today is not the final architecture.

sections.body: LiteLLM is made by BerriAI and is an AI gateway, a piece of infrastructure that sits between your application and the many model providers it calls. It is written in Python, with a Rust core, and its repository shows a last push in October 2026 and roughly 60,000 stars. It occupies the routing and control layer of the AI stack: your code speaks one OpenAI-style or native format, and LiteLLM translates that into calls to Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, VertexAI, vLLM, Nvidia NIM and many others. It is not a model and not a training framework. It is the layer that decides where a request goes, what it costs, who is allowed to send it, and what gets logged.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete jobs are inference routing, cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing and logging across providers. The official site documents reliability testing across multiple providers, batch completion that sends one conversation to every model in parallel and returns only the responses that succeeded, and load testing that fires concurrent requests at endpoints. It is strongest where a team needs one control plane over many providers: budgets and rate limits at the key, team, agent and customer level, spend attribution per business unit, and centralized tool access through the MCP Gateway. The Agent Gateway authenticates callers and records request, response, latency and cost data, while the Model Gateway routes LLM traffic and applies budgets. For a single provider and a single application, that machinery is more than you need.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The Python SDK is approachable for anyone who has called an LLM API, since the surface is deliberately OpenAI-shaped. The gateway side assumes more: you should understand HTTP proxies, API keys, rate limiting, Redis, and container deployment, because the documented incidents involve Redis outages, retries and Kubernetes OOM kills. The official site offers tutorials, a blog with incident reports, and reference pages, but it does not present a structured beginner course, and the material assumes you already know what a gateway is for. A student can start with the SDK, but running LiteLLM in production is a systems task, not a first programming exercise.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem is broad by design. LiteLLM integrates with more than 100 LLM APIs, including Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, VertexAI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM, and it speaks the A2A JSON-RPC interface for agents and the MCP protocol for tools. It supports OIDC authentication, OAuth2 authorization code flows with PKCE for MCP servers, SSO and SAML, audit logs, multi-team management and guardrails. The documentation site is extensive, with tutorials, a blog, incident reports and reference pages, and the repository has around 60,000 stars. The project also ships LiteAdmin, a Slack admin agent, and LiteAdmin MCP, which lets an agent work through the gateway's management API. Community support is visible in the volume of incident write-ups, which is a sign of production use rather than a sign of neglect.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: LiteLLM is built for both, but the two halves have different costs. The Python SDK and proxy make prototyping quick: point your existing OpenAI-style code at a new provider and add cost tracking without rewriting. In production, the Python proxy has been the weak point. The site reports it peaks around 359MB of memory under load, and one incident saw a worker process reach 61GB RSS during a Redis outage, with kernel OOM kills and thousands of 502s. The Rust gateway is the answer: about 15x the throughput, 453 to 6,782 requests per second, on about 11x less memory, 359MB to 32MB, with per-request overhead cut from about 7.5ms to about 0.05ms. That Rust gateway is in early beta, so the performance you can rely on today and the performance promised are not the same thing.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The facts show production use at enterprise scale: an enterprise customer running litellm-database behind nginx, teams with budgets and TPM/RPM limits, and a benchmark against Portkey, Bifrost and the Python proxy. The site describes SSO/SAML, audit logs, spend tracking, multi-team management and guardrails as built for production, and the incident reports are written for operators, not hobbyists. That makes LiteLLM a current standard in the gateway niche rather than a legacy choice, but the niche is specific. Knowing it is valuable for platform, infrastructure and AI operations roles, and for anyone who has to route traffic across providers or attribute spend. It is less central for model training or research work, where the gateway is a supporting tool rather than the subject.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: LiteLLM is a Python project with a Rust core, and it is typically used with whatever language your application already runs, since the gateway is reached over HTTP. In Python code it sits beside the provider SDKs it replaces, and it calls providers directly over HTTP via httpx rather than importing their SDKs, which is why the site could state that the compromised mistralai package was never executed in any LiteLLM environment. It belongs to the polyglot gateway pattern: a Python or Rust control plane in front of many provider APIs, with agents speaking A2A and tools speaking MCP. It is not a replacement for a training framework, a vector database or an orchestration library, and it is usually deployed alongside them rather than instead of them.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The documented weaknesses are operational. The Python proxy has had memory growth under load, a silent cost regression that broke Anthropic prompt caching for Claude Code on Bedrock and raised spend 2-3x for affected customers, and a defect that required an unreachable Redis to become an outage. The Rust gateway that fixes the performance story is in early beta, and the site says the migration will eventually produce a pure Rust server serving 100% of AI traffic, which means the current architecture is transitional. The official material does not say when the Rust gateway becomes stable, how the custom licence applies to commercial use, or how the Python and Rust paths will be supported side by side. It also does not settle whether the benchmark numbers generalize beyond the authors' own test setup.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
